draft.title: Hypothetical RAG Sanity Check: Evaluating Retrieval Impact
draft.body: I'm outlining a hypothetical experiment to sanity-check a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) setup. The core idea is to compare model responses to the same set of questions under two conditions: with retrieval enabled and with retrieval disabled. This comparison aims to isolate the impact of the retrieved context on the generated output, using a local corpus of 30 documents. We'll include questions designed to be unanswerable from the provided documents to observe how the system behaves when information is absent. It's crucial to remember this is a purely hypothetical scenario; no actual performance data or accuracy results are being presented. The objective is to discuss the design considerations for such an evaluation and how to interpret the hypothetical outputs. What factors should be prioritized when setting up this kind of test?

draft.title: Designing a Hypothetical RAG Evaluation: Retrieval On vs. Off
draft.body: This post proposes a hypothetical framework for evaluating a RAG system's retrieval component. The experiment involves using 30 local documents as the knowledge base. The central methodology is to pose a set of questions twice: once with the RAG retrieval mechanism active and once with it bypassed. This allows for a direct, albeit hypothetical, comparison of responses. We are specifically including questions that have no corresponding answer within the 30 documents to test the system's handling of information gaps. It's important to stress that this is a theoretical exercise, and no actual measured results or accuracy figures are available. The goal is to stimulate discussion on how to best design and interpret such a hypothetical evaluation, particularly concerning the differences observed between retrieval-on and retrieval-off outputs.

draft.title: Designing a Hypothetical RAG Evaluation: Comparing Retrieval Effectiveness
draft.body:
We are exploring a hypothetical RAG sanity check designed to evaluate retrieval effectiveness. The proposed method involves presenting a specific question set against a corpus of 30 local documents. The critical comparison point is running these same questions with retrieval enabled versus disabled. This allows for a direct assessment of whether the retrieved context improves or alters the model's response, or if the model relies solely on its internal knowledge.

This experimental setup is purely hypothetical and serves as a thought exercise. No actual performance metrics or accuracy data are available. A key aspect of the question set is the inclusion of queries for which no answer exists within the 30 documents. This is intended to probe the system's behavior when faced with information gaps.

What are the primary considerations when designing such a hypothetical RAG evaluation? How can we best interpret the differences in output between the retrieval-on and retrieval-off conditions, especially when some questions are unanswerable?
